title: LOT’S DAUGHTERS GOT THEIR FATHER DRUNK AND SLEPT WITH HIM—WHY IS THIS HORRIFYING STORY IN THE BIBLE?
paragraphs:
LOT’S DAUGHTERS GOT THEIR FATHER DRUNK AND SLEPT WITH HIM—WHY IS THIS HORRIFYING STORY IN THE BIBLE?
Genesis 19:30–38 is not a story God gave us to excuse human depravity. It is a story He refused to hide—and buried inside its darkness is a trail that eventually leads somewhere almost unbelievable: toward Ruth, toward David, and ultimately toward Jesus Christ.
There are Bible stories people put on nursery walls.
Noah’s ark.
David and Goliath.
Daniel among the lions.
And then there are passages like Genesis 19:30–38.
The passages people read quietly.
The passages preachers may hesitate to touch.
The passages that make you stop, stare at the page, and wonder:
Why is this in the Bible?
A father.
Two daughters.
A cave.
Wine.
Two nights.
Two pregnancies.
Incest.
And somehow this is part of Holy Scripture.
But perhaps the first thing we need to understand is this:
The Bible is holy not because every human action it records is holy.
The Bible is holy because the God who speaks through it tells the truth—even when the truth about humanity is horrifying.
Scripture does not airbrush its heroes.
It does not sanitize dysfunctional families.
It does not pretend believers never collapse.
It does not delete the chapters that would embarrass the family.
And Genesis 19 is one of those chapters.
Lot had just escaped Sodom.
The city was gone.
His wife was gone.
His former life was gone.
The man who had once looked across the Jordan valley and chosen what appeared prosperous now found himself living with his daughters in a cave.
That image alone should stop us.
Lot had escaped the fire...
but escaping a city is not necessarily the same thing as escaping what the city has done to you.
The New Testament astonishingly calls Lot a righteous man who was deeply distressed by the lawlessness surrounding him.
That means we should resist the simplistic temptation to turn Lot into a cartoon villain.
But we should also resist the opposite mistake.
Being distressed by a corrupt culture does not mean that culture has had no influence on you.
You can hate what surrounds you and still carry wounds from living around it.
You can leave Sodom...
and discover that some of Sodom followed you into the cave.
Lot’s daughters looked at their circumstances and reached a terrifying conclusion.
Their father was old. They saw no available husbands. Their future appeared closed. Their family line appeared doomed.
So they decided to manufacture a future for themselves.

Genesis records their reasoning: they would intoxicate their father and use him to preserve offspring through him. The Hebrew idea behind their stated purpose is striking: וּנְחַיֶּה מֵאָבִינוּ זָרַע — unechayyeh me’avinu zeraʿ, essentially, “that we may preserve offspring/seed from our father.”
The word זֶרַע — zeraʿ means “seed” or “offspring.”
They wanted a future.
But instead of trusting God with the future, they attempted to produce one through sin.
And suddenly this ancient cave becomes frighteningly modern.
Because most of us will never do what Lot’s daughters did.
But many of us understand the temptation underneath it.
“What if God doesn’t come through?”
“What if I never get married?”
“What if I never have children?”
“What if this opportunity disappears?”
“What if I lose everything?”
“What if there is no other way?”
Fear starts talking.
Then fear starts reasoning.
Then fear starts calling compromise necessary.
And eventually a person can do something he once considered unthinkable while telling himself he had no other choice.
That is one of the terrifying lessons of this passage:
Fear can become a terrible theologian.
It can make God appear smaller than your circumstances.
It can convince you that obedience is impossible because the future looks impossible.
And once you believe that, sin begins offering itself as a survival strategy.
The daughters make Lot drunk.
The older daughter goes first.
The text says he was unaware of her lying down and getting up.
Then morning comes.
And perhaps this is one of the darkest details of all:
They do it again.
The following night the younger daughter does the same.
Genesis does not celebrate this.
It does not command this.
It does not present incest as acceptable.

In fact, when Israel later receives explicit covenant legislation concerning sexual relationships, sexual relations among close relatives are expressly prohibited. Leviticus 18 opens that section with the prohibition against approaching close kin for sexual relations.
So never confuse biblical description with biblical prescription.
When Scripture tells you Cain murdered Abel, it is not endorsing murder.
When Scripture tells you David committed adultery, it is not endorsing adultery.
When Scripture tells you Peter denied Jesus, it is not endorsing denial.
And when Genesis tells you what happened inside Lot’s cave, God is not calling evil good.
He is showing us something Christianity has never needed to hide:
Human beings desperately need redemption.
The Bible could have edited this family history.
God could have given us a polished book filled with polished people whose lives always made faith look respectable.
Instead, Scripture gives us Noah drunk.
Abraham afraid.
Jacob deceptive.
Judah compromised.
David adulterous and murderous.
Peter denying Christ.
Thomas doubting.
Disciples arguing about greatness.
And Lot’s family sitting in the wreckage of Sodom making catastrophic decisions.
Why?
Because the Bible is not ultimately the story of impressive people climbing their way toward God.
It is the story of a holy God pursuing, judging, rescuing, correcting, forgiving, transforming, and redeeming sinful people.
And now the story becomes even stranger.
Both daughters become pregnant.
The older daughter gives birth to a son.
She calls him מוֹאָב — Mo’av, Moab.

Genesis deliberately associates that name with his scandalous origin—“from [my] father.” The younger daughter names her son בֶּן־עַמִּי — Ben-ʿAmmi, commonly understood as “son of my people/kinsman.” Genesis identifies these sons as ancestors of the Moabites and Ammonites.
Imagine carrying a name connected to the circumstances of your conception.
Imagine having your beginning associated with a cave nobody wants to discuss.
Moab enters Scripture under a shadow.
And if Genesis 19 were the final chapter of the story, perhaps darkness would get the last word.
But keep reading your Bible.
Because generations later...
a woman walks out of Moab.
Her name is Ruth.
Yes.
A Moabite.
A descendant of the people whose biblical origin story reaches back to this horrifying cave.
Ruth loses her husband.
She could remain in Moab.
Instead she clings to Naomi and makes one of Scripture’s great declarations of covenant loyalty.
Naomi’s people will become her people.
Naomi’s God will become her God.
And Ruth eventually meets Boaz.
Boaz redeems.
Ruth becomes his wife.
A son is born.
His name is Obed.
Obed becomes the father of Jesse.
Jesse becomes the father of David.
And then...
centuries later...
Matthew begins telling the story of Jesus Christ.
And Ruth is there.
Matthew 1:5 names her.
“Boaz begat Obed of Ruth...”
The Moabite woman is inside the genealogy of the Messiah.
Do you see what just happened?
Genesis 19 gives us a cave filled with shame.
Ruth gives us a Moabite woman kneeling beneath the wings of Israel’s God.
Matthew gives us Jesus Christ.
The Bible does not say the incest became good.
It never did.
Grace does not rename evil as righteousness.
Grace does something infinitely more beautiful.
God can redeem people whose histories contain evil without approving the evil that shaped those histories.
That distinction matters.
Because somebody reading this has spent years believing your beginning disqualified your ending.
Maybe your family history is ugly.
Maybe your father failed you.
Maybe your mother wounded you.
Maybe addiction ran through your home.
Maybe adultery shattered it.
Maybe you were conceived in circumstances nobody talks about.
Maybe abuse left scars you still struggle to explain.
Maybe you made decisions you would give anything to undo.
Maybe there is a chapter in your life you hope nobody ever reads aloud.
Listen carefully.
Jesus is not intimidated by your genealogy.
He is not frightened by your family history.
He is not standing outside your mess wondering whether His grace is powerful enough to enter.
The gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that the Son of God went to Calvary.
But grace is so powerful that the Son of God rose again.
Christianity does not say, “What happened doesn’t matter.”
Christianity says something far stronger:
What happened does not have to be your master anymore.
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
It does not have the authority to become your god.
Your family may have handed you patterns.
You do not have to worship them.
Your parents may have given you brokenness.
Jesus can give you a new identity.
Your history may have written the opening paragraphs.
Jesus Christ still has authority over the ending.
That is why Genesis 19 belongs in the Bible.
Not because God wants us fascinated by scandal.
Because God wants us sober about sin.
Because He wants us to understand what fear can do when it stops trusting Him.
Because He wants us to see how compromise can travel through families.
Because He refuses to lie about human darkness.
And because when we finally understand how dark human darkness actually is, grace stops looking sentimental.
Grace becomes astonishing.
Maybe you have wondered why the Bible contains so many broken people.
Perhaps the better question is:
What kind of Bible would people like us need?
A Bible filled only with flawless humans would leave sinners with nowhere to stand.
But Scripture gives us people who lied.
People who failed.
People who ran.
People who lusted.
People who doubted.
People whose families were dysfunctional.
People whose histories were embarrassing.
And then Scripture points beyond all of them.
To Jesus.
He is not another broken patriarch needing rescue.
He is the Rescuer.
He is not another sinner hoping grace can cover Him.
He is the Lamb of God who bears sin.
He does not merely enter a broken human story.
He comes to redeem broken human beings.
This is where the story must become personal.
Because it is easy to stare into Lot’s cave and whisper, “How could they?”
It is harder to let Scripture turn the question around.
What have you done because you were afraid God would not provide?
What compromise did you justify because waiting hurt?
What relationship did you enter because loneliness became louder than obedience?
What habit do you keep feeding because pain convinced you that you need it?
What secret are you hiding because shame told you exposure would destroy you?
What have you called “necessary” that God calls sin?
Do not use Lot’s daughters as an excuse to feel morally superior.
Let their story become a warning.
Sin does not need you to become an atheist.
Sometimes it only needs you to become frightened enough to stop trusting God.
But if conviction is rising inside you right now, do not confuse conviction with condemnation.
Run toward Christ.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you out of the cave.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the compromise.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the sexual sin.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the thing you are terrified somebody will discover.
You do not clean yourself before coming to the cross.
You come because you cannot clean yourself.
Jesus Christ was crucified for sinners.
He rose from the dead.
Forgiveness is not pretending sin never mattered.
Forgiveness is possible because Christ paid for sin.
And when a sinner turns to Christ in repentance and faith, the deepest identity of that person no longer has to be the scandal behind them.
Grace can write what shame never could.
Someone reading the comments may discover they are not the only person fighting.
Someone may pray because you were honest.
Someone may return to Christ because your testimony reminded them that grace still reaches people in caves.
Not because Genesis 19 is pleasant.
Come back and remember Ruth.
Come back and remember the genealogy.
Come back and remember the cross.
Not as religious decoration.
Send it to the believer who has disappeared.
Send it to the person who thinks Christianity is only for people who have their lives together.
Even send it to the skeptic who believes the Bible hides from the ugliness of real human life.
It doesn't.
Scripture walks straight into the cave.
And then it keeps walking until the story reaches Christ.
Supporting Gospel work should never replace giving faithfully, serving your local church, caring for your family, or helping people in need.
Because somewhere tonight there is still a person sitting emotionally in a cave.
Ashes behind them.
Fear around them.
Shame inside them.
Convinced the worst chapter has already determined the final sentence.
But Genesis 19 was not the end of the biblical story.
Moab was not the end.
The scandal was not the end.
Ruth came.
David came.
And in the fullness of time...
Jesus came.
And that is the truth shame desperately hopes you never understand:
The chapter you are most ashamed of may be part of your history—but when Jesus becomes Lord of your life, it does not get to be your final author.
